obtained.how: agency PDF from MDIFW's own server: the cited www.maine.gov path refuses scripts (403), but www1.maine.gov serves the same file with the folder written in lower case (ifw)

bibliography.checked_against: the cover and table of contents (PDF pp. 1-2)
bibliography.corrections: Title is 'Inland Fisheries and Hatcheries Strategic Management Plan 2021–2035, Volume III: Species Assessments' (not 'Statewide Fisheries and Hatcheries Management Plan'). The smallmouth material is in section II 'Black Bass' (smallmouth and largemouth), pp. 6–11 (brook trout begins p. 12); pp. 6–10 covers the smallmouth parts. Working URL: https://www1.maine.gov/ifw/docs/21-MDIFW-8-Fisheries-Plan_V3.pdf

claims.claim: smallmouth bass occur in 517 surveyed Maine lakes, 84 of them in the Penobscot region
claims.source_value: 517 lakes and ponds statewide (2020); 84 in Fisheries Management Region F (76 % of Region F's surveyed lake/pond acreage)
claims.quote: now occur in 517 Maine lakes and ponds (Table 2)
claims.conditions: statewide distribution of lakes and ponds containing smallmouth bass, 2020
claims.note: Table 2 row read on the raw text: 'F 84 76%'; statewide total 517 (59 % of surveyed acreage). The plan labels the region only 'F'; that Region F is the Penobscot region comes from MDIFW's regional naming (paper §2.1), not from this document. 'Surveyed lakes' is the paper's wording; the plan says 'lakes and ponds'.

claims.claim: 84 of the 517 smallmouth lakes are in Region F (Penobscot)
MDIFW states that young bass under about 56 mm (2.2 in) do not survive their first winter
claims.location: p. 6 (PDF p. 8), Black Bass: smallmouth bass
claims.quote: bass less than about 2.2 inches long do not survive their first winter
claims.conditions: MDIFW multi-year study of young-of-year bass on waters in southern, central and eastern Maine; the length type (total length presumably) is not stated; 2.2 in = 55.9 mm
claims.note: The same paragraph gives the 'approximately 200+ day starvation period' of the first winter 'when water temperatures fall below 50°F' (which §3.6.8 credits to Jordan 2001: this plan says it too), and adds that after a year of poor survival the next year classes grew and survived better. p. 7 (PDF p. 9): first-season lengths are typically 2.2–2.9 in, fast growers 4+ in.

notes: Values confirmed; only the title and page range in the bibliography need fixing. Useful extras in the same section: males mature at 3–4 yr, females 4–5 (p. 6); a trophy smallmouth (≥18 in) may be 15–20+ yr old (p. 6); first-summer length 2.2–2.9 in in most Maine waters (p. 7).
